title: Binary Search
definition: Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding an element in a sorted array. It works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. If the value of the search key is less than the item in the middle of the interval, narrow the interval to the lower half. Otherwise, narrow it to the upper half.
conceptExplanation: Binary search requires the array to be sorted. It compares the target value to the middle element. If they are not equal, the half in which the target cannot lie is eliminated, and the search continues on the remaining half until the value is found or the interval is empty. Time complexity is O(log n).
keyPoints: - Requires sorted array - Divide and conquer approach - Compares with middle element - Eliminates half at each step - O(log n) time complexity
importantTerminology: Binary Search, Sorted Array, Search Interval, Low, High, Mid, Not Found
workingPrinciple: Initialize low = 0 and high = n-1. While low <= high: calculate mid = Math.floor((low + high) / 2). If arr[mid] == target, return mid. If arr[mid] < target, set low = mid + 1. If arr[mid] > target, set high = mid - 1. If loop ends, return -1 (not found).
realLifeExample: Looking up a word in a dictionary, finding a name in a sorted phone book, searching in a sorted database index
dsaExample: Searching for value 42 in sorted array [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]
diagram: Binary search on array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20, 25] searching for 16: initial range [0-6], mid=3 (value 12), 16>12 so range [4-6], mid=5 (value 20), 16<20 so range [4-4], mid=4 (value 16) found
algorithm:
Binary Search Algorithm:
1. SET low = 0
2. SET high = n - 1
3. WHILE low <= high
   SET mid = floor((low + high) / 2)
   IF arr[mid] == target
     RETURN mid
   ELSE IF arr[mid] < target
     SET low = mid + 1
   ELSE
     SET high = mid - 1
   END IF
4. END WHILE
5. RETURN -1 (not found)

Non-recursive implementation as above.

Recursive binary search passes low and high as parameters.
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  FUNCTION binarySearch(arr, target)
    low = 0
    high = length(arr) - 1
    WHILE low <= high
      mid = floor((low + high) / 2)
      IF arr[mid] == target
        RETURN mid
      ELSE IF arr[mid] < target
        low = mid + 1
      ELSE
        high = mid - 1
      END IF
    END WHILE
    RETURN -1
  END FUNCTION

  // Recursive version\n  FUNCTION binarySearchRecursive(arr, target, low, high)
    IF low > high
      RETURN -1
    END IF
    mid = floor((low + high) / 2)
    IF arr[mid] == target
      RETURN mid
    ELSE IF arr[mid] < target
      RETURN binarySearchRecursive(arr, target, mid + 1, high)
    ELSE
      RETURN binarySearchRecursive(arr, target, low, mid - 1)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION
END
complexity:
Time: O(log n) - each step halves the search interval\nSpace: O(1) for non-recursive, O(log n) for recursive (call stack)
Compared to O(n) for sequential/linear search on sorted data
applications: Searching in large sorted datasets, database indexing, finding position in sorted array, implementing search in JavaScript's built-in methods
advantages: Much faster than linear search on sorted data, O(log n) complexity, simple implementation
limitations: Requires sorted array, cannot be used on unsorted data without sorting first, not suitable for dynamic datasets where frequent sorting needed
commonMistakes: Mid calculation overflow with large arrays (use low + (high - low) / 2), off-by-one errors in low/high updates, forgetting sorted requirement, returning wrong index
importantExamPoints:
Non-recursive vs recursive implementation
Time complexity O(log n) vs O(n) for linear search
Requires sorted array precondition
Edge cases: first occurrence, last occurrence, not found

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain binary search algorithm with non-recursive and recursive implementations.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
Binary search finds an element in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. 

Algorithm: Initialize low = 0, high = n-1. While low <= high: compute mid = floor((low + high) / 2). If arr[mid] == target, return mid. If arr[mid] < target, search right half (low = mid + 1). If arr[mid] > target, search left half (high = mid - 1). If loop ends, return -1.

Non-recursive: Uses while loop, O(1) space.
Recursive: Calls itself with updated low/high parameters, O(log n) space for call stack.

Key advantage: O(log n) time vs O(n) for linear search. Requires sorted array. Mid calculation: Math.floor((low + high) / 2) or low + Math.floor((high - low) / 2) to avoid overflow.

Example: Searching 16 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20, 25]: Step 1: low=0, high=6, mid=3 (value 12), 16>12. Step 2: low=4, high=6, mid=5 (value 20), 16<20. Step 3: low=4, high=4, mid=4 (value 16), found at index 4.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain binary search algorithm, complexity analysis, and compare with linear search.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Binary search algorithm: Given a sorted array of n elements, find the target value. Initialize low = 0, high = n-1. While low <= high: compute mid = floor((low + high) / 2). Compare arr[mid] with target. If equal, return mid. If arr[mid] < target, set low = mid + 1 (search right half). If arr[mid] > target, set high = mid - 1 (search left half). If loop terminates, return -1 (not found).

Complexity Analysis:
- Best case: O(1) - target is at middle
- Average case: O(log n)
- Worst case: O(log n) - target not present or at extremes
- Space: O(1) non-recursive, O(log n) recursive (call stack)

Comparison with Linear Search:
- Linear search: O(n) time, works on sorted/unsorted, simple, no preprocessing needed
- Binary search: O(log n) time, requires sorted array, slightly more complex, needs sorted precondition
- For n = 1000: linear ~1000 comparisons, binary ~10 comparisons
- For n = 1,000,000: linear ~1,000,000, binary ~20

Optimizations: Use low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid integer overflow. For finding first/last occurrence, modify comparison conditions.

Applications: Database indexing, finding square root, exponentiation, numerical methods.
